A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Cubeworld fine-tuning study. Their complete main texts, figures, equations and appendices are readable and support comparison despite the changed title, model selection and figure numbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original Qwen2-VL fine-tuning experiments, generalization evaluations and human-judgment studies, with results in Sections 3.1–3.6 and Appendices E–G.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental and human-judgment results and reports additional Llama evaluations and the paired-pyramid transfer experiment in Section 3.4 and Figure 4.

M1.justification: The QLoRA intervention, cross-entropy objective, adapted vision/language layers and Yes/No scoring procedure are retained. Applying this procedure to Llama models expands the experimental model set; no new fine-tuning algorithm or architectural modification is introduced.

E1.justification: The existing Cubeworld tasks, Lerer naturalistic images and human datasets remain. V2 adds a restricted paired-pyramid scenario in which removing the red block creates a factual-stability test image corresponding to a causal-training image (Section 3.4, Figure 4). This extends input conditions within the existing cognitive domains.

E2.justification: V2 Figure 2 adds GPT-4o as an evaluated comparator, with reported accuracies across the three evaluation datasets. Base-model and human reference results, already represented elsewhere in v1, are also displayed alongside the fine-tuned models in the expanded heatmap.

E3.justification: The evaluated model set changes from Qwen2-VL 2B/7B to Qwen2-VL 7B and Llama 3.2 11B/90B. Main heatmap and alignment comparisons switch to 11B, while appendix learning trajectories switch to 90B. The new paired-image experiment tests transformed training configurations with an explicit red-block-removal prompt. Existing training budgets and core hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds a substantial diagnostic control: causal-trained models must judge factual stability on corresponding pyramid images with the red block removed, alongside an unseen-causal-stimulus evaluation (Figure 4). This directly investigates whether cross-task failure persists when visual differences are minimized. Existing generalization and learning-trajectory analyses are also revised for the larger model set.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over three seeds, Wilson score intervals for accuracy plots, and bootstrapped 95% intervals using 10,000 subsamples for agreement analyses. V2 reiterates the seed procedure and relocates the bootstrap description to Appendix D; it does not establish additional runs or a changed uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: V2 adds Llama and GPT-4o results, removes 2B results, and replaces the main Qwen7B heatmap/alignment results and appendix learning trajectories with other models. For example, human-tuned agreement on Cubeworld/Lerer is 0.35/0.31 for Qwen7B in v1 versus 0.37/0.37 for Llama11B in v2; these are different-model results. New Figure 4 reports approximately 0.83–0.90 causal accuracy but roughly chance-level matched factual transfer.

T1.justification: The adapter mathematics, softmax formula and agreement definition are unchanged. The agreement equation moves from Section 3.5 to Appendix D. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the new mechanism discussions do not introduce formal mathematical results.

C1.justification: V2 explicitly narrows the abstract and concluding generalization claims to task-specific fine-tuning, with the conclusion specifying parameter-efficient fine-tuning. The central contributions and findings—within-task improvement, improved human alignment and limited transfer—remain.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the paired-image failure as evidence of task-specific shortcuts and adds binding-problem and supervised-memorization versus reinforcement-learning hypotheses. It explicitly acknowledges that joint models were not tested on a third cognitive task and that broader task distributions might help. Appendix D also adds an explanation for model–human agreement exceeding human–human agreement.

D1.justification: V2 documents the paired-image construction and removal prompt, but removes v1's Qwen architecture/pretraining description. Its alignment-figure caption also no longer identifies the joint model's exact training split. Core fine-tuning hyperparameters, hardware and analysis-software versions remain documented.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens the research context beyond the original neighboring fine-tuning studies. Section 1.1 adds neurosymbolic visual reasoning and mathematical/compositional generalization; the introduction and discussion add binding-problem research and supervised-versus-reinforcement-learning explanations. These additions introduce substantive relationships to alternative approaches and mechanisms.

P1.justification: V2 changes the title to emphasize visual cognition, edits several paragraphs to lead with findings, condenses captions and adds an Impact Statement. Agreement-analysis details move to Appendix D, and the pretraining appendix is removed. The main section organization and much of the prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds the four-panel paired-image Figure 4 and expands Figure 2 with comparator rows. Main and appendix plots revise model legends, visual encodings and some axis ranges for the expanded comparisons. Figure 1 is relocated and captions are revised; the appendix stimulus examples are retained with new numbering.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central transfer evidence by testing a second model family up to 90B parameters and adding the paired-image control in Section 3.4. These changes address v1's reliance on small Qwen models and reduce visual differences that could explain cross-task failure. More explicit claim boundaries improve calibration. These gains outweigh the removal of 2B results and some model/split documentation, although the proposed mechanisms remain hypotheses.
